text: Was the repeated line spoken by a non-human animal (such as a parrot)?
Did the same single person say the repeated line all seven times?
Were the seven repetitions spoken over seven separate occasions (e.g., seven visits or departures) rather than all at once?
Is the "you" in the repeated line addressed to the narrator?
Is the narrator the one who caused the speaker's disappointment (i.e., the narrator is the guilty party who wronged the speaker)?
Is the sentence being said as part of a romantic breakup or lover's quarrel between the speaker and the person addressed?
Is the line being practiced or performed as a scripted/acted line (rehearsal or performance), rather than a genuine spontaneous farewell?
Is the fact that the line is repeated exactly seven times important to the puzzle's solution (rather than just emphasis)?
Is the narrator a dependent or subordinate of the departing speaker (e.g., a child, employee, or patient) who will suffer because that person is leaving?
Is the narrator something other than a human person (e.g., a machine, AI, program, or fictional character)?
Is there a third individual present who is the real target of the disappointment (the line also caught the narrator up in it)?
After the speaker leaves, will the narrator be blamed or punished by other people (someone other than the departing speaker) for that departure?
Does the repeated line reach the narrator indirectly (via phone, voicemail, recording, radio, or written message) rather than face-to-face?
Is the narrator a professional providing a service to the speaker (doctor, teacher, therapist, lawyer, shopkeeper, etc.)?
Are the narrator and the speaker members of the same family (related by blood or marriage)?
Is the narrator elderly, ill, or otherwise in a condition where they need care from others?
Is the speaker the narrator's child (son or daughter)?
Is this scene taking place during a game or competition (the "never coming back" being a frustrated outburst rather than a literal permanent departure)?
Is the speaker the narrator's parent (mother or father)?
Is the speaker blaming the narrator for something the narrator did not actually do (a misunderstanding or misattribution)?
Is the speaker the narrator's sibling (brother or sister)?
Will the narrator suffer a serious practical loss (being left alone, losing a home, or losing financial support) as a result of this family member leaving for good?
Is the narrator a child or minor (under 18)?
Is the disappointment about a misfortune or situation the narrator is in (something that happened to the narrator), rather than a deliberate action the narrator chose to take?
Is the speaker dying or about to die, so "I'm never coming back" refers to death rather than merely leaving?
Was it a child (such as the narrator's own child) whose behavior caused the relative's disappointment, with the narrator being addressed as the responsible adult?
Is the relative's "you" referring to the narrator as a representative or stand-in for a group or another person, rather than to the narrator personally?
Is "I know I'm in trouble" referring to legal or criminal trouble (e.g., facing the police or prosecution)?
Does the relative's departure directly worsen the narrator's legal situation (e.g., the relative was a witness, an alibi, or a bail surety/guarantor for the narrator)?
Is the narrator's legal trouble caused by an actual illegal act the narrator has committed (rather than a false accusation)?
Is the relative disappointed and leaving because they have learned about the narrator's illegal act?
Is the same act both the source of the relative's disappointment and the narrator's illegal act — the relative knows of the act and is disappointed, but does not know it is criminal?
Is the narrator already in custody or detained (in prison or jail) when the relative says this, so "I'm never coming back" means the relative will not visit again?
Are the relative's "never coming back" departure and the narrator's legal trouble part of one connected chain of events, rather than two unrelated incidents?
Did the narrator's own personal choice or action (a legitimate life decision, not a wrong against the relative) cause the relative's disappointment?
Did the narrator commit the illegal act by exploiting the relative — using the relative's identity, name, accounts, or property without consent?
Was the narrator's illegal act a violent crime (such as murder or assault)?
Was the victim of the narrator's violent act a member of the same family?
Does the family believe the murdered relative simply went away or disappeared, rather than knowing they were killed?
Was the murdered family member someone close to the departing relative (such as that relative's spouse, child, or parent)?
Is the departing relative — the person who says "You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back" — the victim of the narrator's violent act?
Was the narrator's violent act a deliberate attack on that relative (rather than an accident)?
Was the narrator attacking that relative in order to stop or protect someone from that relative (e.g., defense of another person)?
Is the victim unaware that it was the narrator who attacked/harmed them?
Is the narrator's legal trouble specifically due to the attack on this relative — i.e., that assault may be reported or prosecuted?
Is the victim of the narrator's attack the narrator's spouse or romantic partner (a domestic-violence situation)?
Is the spouse leaving and cutting ties forever because the narrator physically attacked/hurt them?
Did the narrator's attack on the spouse occur shortly before this farewell (recently), rather than long ago?
Did the narrator's attack leave the spouse with a lasting injury or illness?
Is the narrator currently in prison or about to be incarcerated for the assault, and does "never coming back" mean the spouse will stop visiting the narrator there?

The narrator is a married adult who has deliberately and violently assaulted their spouse — a family member by marriage, and the very person who speaks here. The spouse survived the attack (apparently without lasting injury) but is deeply let down and announces "You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back," permanently leaving the marriage and cutting ties for good. The narrator, watching the spouse walk out, sighs "Sigh, I know I'm in trouble": they recognize that the assault is now bound to come to light and be reported/prosecuted, so they face criminal legal consequences — though they are not yet arrested or imprisoned. In short: a violent assault on the spouse leads to the spouse's permanent departure and severed relationship, and the narrator's realization of impending legal trouble for that assault.
Did the narrator attack the spouse AFTER the spouse announced they were leaving ("I'm never coming back") — i.e., the violence was a reaction to being left?
Is the spouse's disappointment about the narrator's ongoing character or behavior (e.g., drinking, gambling, dishonesty, neglect), rather than a single isolated incident?
Is this a literal, present-day, real-world domestic situation (rather than a metaphor, dream, historical, or fantasy setting)?
Is someone other than the spouse aware of the narrator's assault (e.g., a witness, or the person who will report it)?
Is the narrator's legal trouble essentially that, once the spouse leaves or disappears, the narrator will be suspected of having harmed the spouse?
Is the spouse leaving in a way that leaves others unaware of their whereabouts (so their disappearance will look like foul play)?
After leaving, will the spouse later be found dead or seriously harmed — which is why suspicion will fall on the narrator?
Will the narrator be suspected of harming the spouse mainly because of the narrator's known history of violence toward the spouse (reputation/record), rather than any new harm?

Did the narrator kill the spouse (the violent act was fatal), so the spouse's repeated "I'm never coming back" and the narrator's "I know I'm in trouble" are the narrator's own imagination or a haunting — i.e., the narrator murdered the spouse and now dreads discovery?
Is the spouse leaving the narrator for another romantic partner (an affair) — a reason separate from the assault?
Is the narrator's "I know I'm in trouble" essentially that they expect to be arrested or prosecuted for the assault they themselves carried out on the spouse?

The narrator is an adult who has deliberately and violently assaulted their spouse — a family member by marriage. The spouse survived the attack without lasting injury. Having had enough, the spouse declares "You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back," leaving the narrator and the marriage for good. The narrator, watching them go, sighs "Sigh, I know I'm in trouble," knowing that their own violent act makes them criminally liable: they expect to be arrested/prosecuted for the assault on the spouse, and they will be the obvious suspect in any harm attributed to the spouse. In short: the narrator's deliberate assault on the spouse is a real, chargeable crime; the spouse's permanent departure leaves the narrator facing the legal consequences of that assault.
Was the narrator's "violent act" actually poisoning or secretly drugging the spouse — a covert act rather than an open beating?

Was the narrator actually defending themselves when they struck the spouse — i.e., the spouse was abusing the narrator, so the narrator never truly "wronged" the spouse but will be the one arrested for assault?
Had the spouse been shielding the narrator from prosecution by never reporting the assault — so that once the spouse leaves for good, the narrator expects the assault to be reported and face arrest?
Is the spouse relocating far away to start over (e.g., abroad or another city), so "I'm never coming back" means a geographic departure rather than a nearby estrangement?
Is the narrator's expected arrest for an assault that is not yet known to the authorities — i.e., the narrator dreads the hidden assault being discovered?

The narrator has secretly and violently assaulted their spouse — a family member by marriage — and this abuse has so far gone unreported and unnoticed by authorities. The spouse, deeply let down, declares "You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back" and leaves the narrator for good. Watching them go, the narrator sighs "I know I'm in trouble": they realize that with the spouse now out of the household and out of their control, the hidden abuse will surface, the narrator will be suspected of having harmed the spouse, and they will face arrest and prosecution for the assault they actually committed. In short: an undiscovered spouse-abuser dreads that the victim's departure will expose the assault and bring criminal consequences.

Is the person the narrator actually attacked someone else in the family (e.g., a child or another relative) — so the spouse is leaving in shock at harm done to that person rather than being the victim themselves?
Does the spouse bear visible signs of injury (e.g., bruises) as they leave, so others who see them will suspect the narrator of having harmed them?
Will the narrator's hidden assault be exposed through a recording or device (e.g., a phone, camera, or smart speaker that captured it), leading to their arrest?
Will the spouse cut off contact with other people (family/friends) as they leave, so the narrator becomes the suspect in the spouse's absence?
Is the narrator's fear that the spouse, now free of them, will finally go to the police and report the abuse — pressing charges?
Was the violent act one that caused the spouse to lose a pregnancy or unborn child (with no lasting physical injury to the spouse herself)?

The narrator is a married adult who has secretly and deliberately assaulted their spouse — a family member by marriage. This assault is still hidden: nobody has reported it, so it is unknown to the authorities. The spouse, worn down and disappointed for reasons of their own, announces "You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back" and leaves the marriage for good. The narrator, watching them go, sighs "Sigh, I know I'm in trouble," because they know that they will be the prime suspect for having harmed the spouse and that the hidden assault they committed can no longer stay buried — it will come to light and they will be arrested and prosecuted for it. In short: a secretly abusive spouse dreads that their unreported assault will be exposed and that they will be blamed and charged for the harm they truly did to their partner.

Did the narrator's violence occur during a consensual activity (sparring, rough play, or an agreed fight) where the narrator went too far — so it wasn't "wronging" the spouse in the ordinary sense yet remains a chargeable assault?
Is the narrator about to be arrested in this very scene (authorities arriving now, or the offense just exposed in this moment)?
Does "I know I'm in trouble" reflect the narrator's own conscience or intent to confess / turn themselves in — rather than being caught by others?
